A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same human-motion calibration and dynamic NeRF work. The main texts and included appendices are readable, and corresponding equations, algorithms, figures, and tables can be matched despite retitling and reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original calibration, novel-view synthesis, ablation, and robustness results on five Panoptic Studio scenes in Section 4, Tables 1–3, and supplementary figures.

after.justification: v2 retains these original results and adds Mobile-Stage reconstruction, EgoBody calibration, and mixed-frame-rate experiments, including supplementary visual results.

M1.justification: v1 explicitly assumes equal frame rates. v2 adds linear interpolation of lower-rate joint trajectories before alignment and interpolation of missing EgoBody frames. These are limited procedural adaptations; SLAHMR extraction, DTW/global alignment, Procrustes calibration, and progressive K-Planes refinement remain.

E1.justification: Coverage expands from single-person, static-camera Panoptic scenes to three-person smartphone recordings in Mobile-Stage and two-person EgoBody scenes containing a moving head-mounted camera alongside static cameras. v2 also evaluates mixed-frame-rate inputs. EgoBody covers initialization only, not full dynamic reconstruction.

E2.justification: The reconstruction comparisons retain Sync-NeRF with ground-truth poses, the calibrated K-Planes oracle, and the no-progressive-training variant. Mobile-Stage uses this same comparison set. The DUSt3R/COLMAP illustration remains; newly cited human-calibration methods are not added as evaluated comparators.

E3.justification: v2 introduces initialization-only evaluation on sparse EgoBody views, using 200-frame clips with at least 90 overlapping frames, and unit-bounding-box translation errors for EgoBody and Mobile-Stage. It adds a 20/1 Mobile-Stage train/test split and a mixed-rate protocol with five 24-FPS videos and the others at 30 FPS. The documented Panoptic sampling, training budget, and test-time optimization remain.

E4.justification: Table 2 adds a test of initialization robustness to mixed frame rates. The progressive-training ablation is also evaluated on Mobile-Stage. Existing human-state-distance, SMPL-noise, and image-degradation analyses are retained with their previous results.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seed-based variability, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Added experiments continue the existing practice of reporting point estimates and averages.

E6.justification: v2 adds calibration results for Mobile-Stage and three EgoBody scenes, mixed-FPS results, and Mobile-Stage rendering results: Table 3 reports 23.27 PSNR for the proposed method, 17.26 for Sync-NeRF, and 22.98 for the oracle. Panoptic Table 3 scores remain unchanged. Table 1's mean Panoptic input offset changes from 62.39 to 30.64 frames without explaining whether this corrects reporting or reflects different data.

T1.justification: The stated problem assumptions now explicitly include known cross-view person correspondences and permit unequal frame rates, replacing v1's equal-rate restriction. The mathematical formulation and Procrustes/alignment algorithms otherwise remain substantively unchanged after renumbering and relocation; no new proof is introduced.

C1.justification: The introduction drops v1's specific average-error claims of less than 0.4 degrees rotation and 0.2 cm translation, replacing them with qualitative accuracy claims over the expanded evaluation. The central human-motion calibration contribution, progressive refinement, and claim of joint dynamic-NeRF reconstruction from unknown offsets and poses remain.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly explains the initialization-only EgoBody evaluation through sparse-view reconstruction difficulty and identifies moving-camera refinement as future work. It removes v1's explanation for omitting refinement on degraded videos. Appendix C introduces an inconsistency by describing EgoBody refinement, although Table 1 and Figure 9 report initialization only.

D1.justification: Appendices A–B add EgoBody clip and missing-frame processing details and specify Mobile-Stage grid resolutions and regularization scheduling. Panoptic undistortion details are relocated. Conversely, v1's explicit first-frame/one-pose-per-static-video implementation description disappears. The project-page link is unchanged.

R1.justification: v2 adds a substantive 'Camera calibration with human' subsection covering CameraHMR, Virtual Correspondence, moving-person calibration, person-reidentification calibration, and HSfM. It acknowledges shared human-based calibration ideas and distinguishes synchronization, camera-motion, and reconstruction assumptions. This materially expands positioning beyond v1's human-pose and NeRF discussions.

P1.justification: v2 drops 'Pattern' from the title, edits and condenses several passages, adds a related-work subsection, and reorganizes supplementary material into dataset, implementation, and result sections. Dataset specifications and Algorithm 1 move to the appendix. The overall narrative and most method exposition remain recognizable.

P2.justification: Figure 5 becomes a multi-dataset calibration display, and new Figures 7, 9, and 10 show Mobile-Stage and EgoBody results. Tables 1 and 3 gain dataset groupings and additional results, while Table 2 gains the mixed-FPS row. Existing Panoptic visual comparisons are retained as Figures 8, 11, and 12 rather than replaced.

improvement.justification: v1 validates the approach only on static, single-person Panoptic scenes. v2 substantially strengthens evidence beyond that setting through multi-person smartphone reconstruction, initialization with sparse and moving cameras, and mixed-rate testing. The expanded discussion of earlier human-based calibration also addresses an important positioning gap. Unexplained Panoptic offset changes and Appendix C's overstatement of EgoBody refinement weaken reporting, but the validation and positioning gains outweigh these limited problems. Full moving-camera reconstruction remains unvalidated.
